sources: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2026, OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications, vendor announcements and independent 2026 reviews

tools.note: Broadest lifecycle coverage: model scanning, red teaming, AI-SPM, runtime firewall, AI gateway and agent security, tied into Palo Alto NGFW. Best when you already run Palo Alto.
Continuous red teaming plus runtime guardrails, with model validation. Fits organisations standardised on Cisco networking and Secure Access.
Developer-friendly LLM firewall with strong prompt injection detection and Lakera Red for testing. Narrower scope: little on model supply chain or posture.
Strong on employee AI use and homegrown app runtime: injection, data leakage, shadow AI and MCP discovery, inside the Singularity XDR console.
FortiAIGate guards LLM traffic (injection, leakage, cost abuse); Virtue AI (acquired Aug 2026) adds agent red teaming, MCP scanning and tool-call blocking. Integration still maturing.
Model-centric security: model file scanning, adversarial ML detection, model theft and poisoning. Good for classic ML and open-weight models; lighter on agents.
Finds AI services, models, data and exposed endpoints across your cloud, and the attack paths between them. Does not block prompts at runtime.
Built for agents and low-code copilots: inventory, posture, runtime guardrails on tool use, permission analysis. Strong on Microsoft Copilot Studio and similar builders.

tools.s: Defender for AI, Prompt Shields, Purview, Entra Agent ID
tools.note: If your AI runs on Azure / M365: Prompt Shields for injection, content safety filters, Purview DLP for prompts, Defender for Cloud AI threat protection, Entra identities for agents.

tools.s: garak, Promptfoo, NeMo Guardrails, LLM Guard
tools.note: Free scanners and guardrail libraries. Good for CI testing and a baseline filter; you own the tuning, scale and operations.

tools.s: WAF, API gateway, SAST/SCA, IAM/PAM, DLP, CSPM, SIEM
tools.note: Still the main control for the traditional rows, and for rate limiting and output sanitising. AI tools add to this layer; they do not replace it.

types.note: Staff using public or licensed chat tools. Main risks are pasting confidential data and unsanctioned tools. Controls: approved tool list, prompt DLP, browser-level AI discovery.

Answers from SharePoint, wikis, manuals. Risks come from the documents: poisoned or injected content, and users seeing data they shouldn't. Controls: permission-aware retrieval, source curation, injection scanning of retrieved text.
Exposed to anyone on the internet. Expect jailbreaks, prompt extraction, abuse of cost and brand-damaging answers. Controls: runtime firewall, topic limits, rate limits, output review for claims.
Reads untrusted repos and issues, holds credentials, installs packages, runs commands. Controls: sandboxed runtimes, scoped tokens, SCA on generated code, approval for pushes and deploys.
Business users build agents fast, often with broad connectors and their own credentials. Controls: agent inventory, connector policies, posture scanning (e.g. Zenity), owner accountability.
Takes real actions in business systems. Risk shifts from what it says to what it does. Controls: per-agent identity, least privilege, tool-call inspection, human approval for irreversible actions.
Agents pass instructions and context to each other, so one compromised step spreads. Controls: trust boundaries between agents, end-to-end tracing, circuit breakers and a kill switch.
You own the model supply chain and infrastructure. Controls: model file scanning, signed artifacts, training-data provenance, GPU host hardening, inference gateway.
Classic ML is less exposed to prompt attacks but open to poisoning, evasion and model theft. Controls: data pipeline integrity, drift monitoring, adversarial robustness testing.
Errors become safety and production incidents. Controls: IT/OT segmentation, hard limits on setpoints, human-in-the-loop, OT monitoring, fail-safe defaults.

risks.w: The chatbot or agent still sits behind a web front end and APIs. WAF, API gateway and DDoS protection do the work; network vendors cover it through their wider portfolio, not their AI product.
AI frameworks ship CVEs like any library. SAST/SCA and container scanning are primary; Wiz and Prisma add cloud-side visibility.

Leaked LLM API keys and over-privileged service accounts are a top real-world cause of AI incidents. IAM/PAM and secret scanning lead; SentinelOne flags secrets in prompts, Zenity and Wiz find exposed credentials.
Exposed inference endpoints, public vector stores and open training buckets. CSPM and AI-SPM (Wiz, Prisma, Defender for Cloud) are the right tools.
Your existing DLP and data classification still matter because AI apps read from the same data. Purview extends naturally to Copilot and Azure OpenAI.
You need AI events (blocked prompts, tool calls) in the SOC. SentinelOne and Microsoft are native to their XDR/SIEM; others export to your SIEM.
The core job of every runtime AI firewall. Detection quality varies by language and attack style; test with Thai and mixed-language prompts.

risks.c: LLM01 · via RAG docs, email, web pages
risks.w: Instructions hidden in content the model reads. Tools must scan retrieved documents and tool responses, not only user input. Lakera, Prisma, Virtue AI and Zenity inspect tool and document content explicitly.

risks.c: LLM02 · PII, secrets in prompts and answers
risks.w: Two directions: staff pasting confidential data into AI, and the model leaking data it can reach. Runtime tools redact both ways; Purview adds labels-aware DLP.
Extraction of system prompts and hidden instructions. Output filters catch it; better still, keep secrets and business logic out of prompts.

risks.c: LLM04 · malicious model files, unvetted weights
risks.w: Pickle-based model files can execute code on load. Model scanners (Protect AI in Prisma, HiddenLayer, Cisco) are essential if you pull from Hugging Face or fine-tune open models.
The weakest-covered row. HiddenLayer is strongest on ML poisoning; for RAG, rely on source control, document provenance and write access to the knowledge base.

risks.c: LLM output into SQL, shell, HTML
risks.w: Treat model output as untrusted input. Output encoding, parameterised queries and sandboxing in your own code do most of the work.

risks.c: LLM06 · cost abuse, denial of wallet
risks.w: Token floods and runaway agent loops burn budget. AI gateways (Prisma via Portkey, FortiAIGate) and API rate limits handle it.
Content filters help with toxicity and topic control. Hallucination is mainly a design problem: grounding, citations and human review for high-stakes answers.
You cannot secure AI you don't know exists. AI-SPM and browser or endpoint discovery (SentinelOne, Prisma, Wiz, Zenity) give the inventory; CASB gives partial coverage.
Relevant to predictive and vision models in plants and logistics, not only LLMs. HiddenLayer is the specialist here.
The biggest climber in OWASP 2026. Look for tools that inspect and block individual tool calls, not just prompts: Prisma AIRS agent security, Virtue AI, Zenity.
Agents need their own identities and least-privilege scopes. Microsoft Entra Agent ID, CyberArk (inside Prisma) and Zenity's permission analysis address this; classic PAM partially.
Tool descriptions can carry injected instructions and MCP servers can be impersonated. Prompt Security, Virtue AI, Prisma and Zenity discover and scan MCP servers.
Planted content in long-term agent memory redirects later sessions. Tooling is immature everywhere; use memory scoping, expiry and review.
Multi-agent chains fail in ways no single check sees. You need behaviour monitoring and a way to cut an agent off. Zenity is furthest along; others are adding it.
